visit.heading: How a visit works
visit.p1: A visit is a walk from stop to stop. At each stop something stands in front of you: a picture, a machine, a book or a place, and a short text.
visit.p2: The text has three layers: the line you read first, a drawer that opens when you want more, and the record, which names the sources.
visit.p3: Here is one stop of the {name} wing: stop {stop}, in front of the Mona Lisa.

stop.heading: One stop, up close
stop.sample_note: The title and the three texts are the museum's own words.

sure.text: Each stop carries one of four grades: documented, reconstructed, conjectural, or not known. The word stands under the stop's title.

what.heading: What this museum is
what.i1_text: Every picture, sheet and machine is a reproduction or a reconstruction, and its label says which. A reproduction is a copy of a picture or a page. A reconstruction is built again from what is left: a sheet, a plan, an old account. Built in code means a program describes every beam and wheel, and the computer draws the picture.
what.i2_text: With the museums, libraries and collections that keep them.
what.i3_text: Every fact in a wing has a source.
what.i4_text: ChipMates gemeinnützige GmbH, a nonprofit. No advertising, nothing for sale.
what.i5_text: No partnership with any museum. ChipMates alone decides what it shows and says.
what.i6_text: On your screen. A website, built once for the phone and once for the desktop.

inst.heading: For museums, libraries and the press
inst.p1: If your institution holds a work shown here, its label names you as the holder, with the source and the licence line of the picture. It claims nothing more.
inst.p2: The page of each wing lists what it shows and names every holder of an original, in one list.
inst.p3: If a credit is wrong, or you have a better picture, write to us and we correct it. The address is in the legal notice. Journalists reach us there too.

closing.heading: Come in and look closely
closing.p: Some places are far away, closed or gone. Here you can walk into one of them, rebuilt as closely as the sources allow.

page_what.title: What this museum is | Museum of Ages, a digital museum
page_what.description: Museum of Ages is a digital museum on the web. What it shows, how sure it is, where the originals are held, how the words are made and who runs it.
page_what.lead: Museum of Ages is a digital museum. This page says plainly what it shows, how it is made and who answers for it.
page_what.m_one: We rebuild what was, one place at a time, and make it as accessible as we can, so that everyone can learn from it.
page_what.m_p1: Many places are far away, closed, crowded or gone. Many people cannot travel to them, cannot pay for a ticket, or cannot stand in front of a painting for long. We want to change that, as far as a website can.
page_what.m_p2: We do not replace the visit or the original. We rebuild a place as it was, as far as we know, and invite you to walk in. One place at a time.
page_what.m_role_1: A first walk, not the visit itself
page_what.m_role_3: A pointer to the museums and libraries that keep the originals
page_what.m_role_4: A complement to school and museum, never a replacement
page_what.m_bar_1_text: No trip needed. You visit from where you are, when you have time.
page_what.m_bar_2_text: No stairs, no queue, no standing, at your own pace.
page_what.m_bar_3_text: Free entry, no account, no ads. A nonprofit runs it.
page_what.m_bar_3_text_before: Free entry, no account, no ads. A nonprofit runs it.
page_what.m_bar_4_text: Plain words, no prior knowledge needed.
page_what.m_not_p: No sound and no spoken words yet. Not yet tested with a screen reader. When that changes, it will say so here.
page_what.m_close: We are glad when a walk here ends in front of the real thing: in Amboise, in a museum, in the reading room of a library. That is not a loss.
page_what.s1_p1: Museum of Ages is a website. It works on a phone and on a desktop, and you need no ticket and no account.
page_what.s1_p2: A wing is one place at one moment, rebuilt in code. A program describes every beam, wheel and stone, and the computer draws the picture from it. You walk through it stop by stop.
page_what.s2_p: Everything shown is one of three things: a reproduction, a reconstruction, or a place the museum designed itself. The label says which.
page_what.s2_a_text: The paintings, drawings and notebook pages are digital copies of works in the public domain. These works are so old that no one holds a copyright in them. Each copy carries the name of its holder, its source and its licence line.
page_what.s2_b_text: The house and the machines are built in code: after Leonardo's sheets, after plans and photographs of the house, and after old accounts. They follow the sources as far as the sources go, and each is labelled as a reconstruction. The furniture in the house is of the period. None of it was his. The halls and courts around the house are the museum's own design.
page_what.honesty: As it was, as far as we know.
page_what.s2_four_p: We always say how sure we are. There are four grades, each with its word and its colour, the same as in the wing, so you can see how firm a statement is. The words in a list of paintings, such as disputed or workshop, are something else: they say who is thought to have made a work.
page_what.s2_four_1_text: A source from the time says it, and we name the source.
page_what.s2_four_2_text: No source says it outright. We worked it out from what the sources give.
page_what.s2_four_3_text: We think so, or a scholar does, and no source says it. Take it as a reasoned guess.
page_what.s2_four_4_text: Nobody knows. We say that too, and we leave the gap open.
page_what.s2_lic_p: Every picture is shown under a licence or a rights note that allows it, and its label names it. These kinds are in the Leonardo da Vinci wing today. The CC letters stand for standard licences of Creative Commons. Each one says what anyone may do with the picture, and what not.
page_what.s2_lic_5: Public domain by age, for old printed copies
page_what.s2_lic_6: Faithful reproductions of public domain works from Wikimedia Commons
page_what.s2_lic_7: Scans of the Bibliothèque de l'Institut de France, CC BY-NC-ND 3.0 FR
page_what.s2_lic_after: Where a holder claims rights in the image of a public domain work, the label says so.
page_what.s3_p1: The originals stay with their holders.
page_what.s3_link: The list of holders for the {name} wing
page_what.s3_p3: Where a work is on loan, or its present place is not confirmed, the list says so.
page_what.s4_made: A person reads, corrects and approves every text before it is published. The drafts are written with AI from a research file that names a source for every fact.
page_what.s4_p1: Each stop has three layers of text: the line you read first, a drawer that opens when you want more, and the record, which names the sources.
page_what.s4_p2: The sources open beside the text.
page_what.s5_p1: Museum of Ages is a project of ChipMates gemeinnützige GmbH, a small German nonprofit in Freiburg. Its purpose is education. Charitable status means we answer to a mission, not to investors.
page_what.s5_p2: The museum is independent. It has no partnership with any museum. ChipMates alone decides what it shows and what it says. The site carries no advertising and sells nothing.
page_what.s5_pays: ChipMates gemeinnützige GmbH pays for the museum.

page_what.s6_p: The museum's code is open source under the AGPL-3.0 or later. The museum's own texts and pictures are under CC BY-SA 4.0: anyone may share and adapt them, commercially too, if they credit the museum, link the licence, mark changes and share adaptations under the same licence. Excluded are works and data of others, such as reproductions, music, quotations and map data, and the museum's name and logo.
page_what.s6_before: The museum's code is not public yet. It will be published under the AGPL-3.0 or a later version, an open source licence. Anyone may then read it, use it and change it under that licence. The copyright in the texts and pictures the museum makes itself lies with ChipMates gemeinnützige GmbH.
page_what.s7_p: The museum is built once for the phone and once for the desktop, in English and German, in plain words. It aims at WCAG 2.2 AA, the common standard for accessible websites. It sets no tracking cookies and does no profiling. The details are on the privacy page.
